name: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 35 (TGM6)
aliases: autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type SCA35

clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant, slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia caused by pathogenic variants in TGM6, which encodes transglutaminase 6, an enzyme expressed in neurons
Typically presents in adulthood with gait unsteadiness and dysarthria, often accompanied by a prominent postural and kinetic tremor, giving a recognisable tremor-ataxia phenotype
Limb incoordination, saccadic pursuit and gaze-evoked nystagmus are common, and some patients develop pyramidal signs with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses
Focal or task-specific features such as torticollis, spasmodic dysphonia or writer's cramp have been reported and can precede overt ataxia
Brain MRI generally shows cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with mild brainstem involvement, but imaging is a supportive rather than a defining feature
Diagnosis rests on molecular confirmation of a TGM6 variant against a background of dominant inheritance; repeat-expansion SCAs should be excluded first as they are far commoner
There is no disease-modifying therapy; care is supportive and multidisciplinary, centred on physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, gait aids and tremor management
reference.pathophysiology: SCA35 arises from heterozygous pathogenic variants in TGM6, which encodes transglutaminase 6, a calcium-dependent enzyme that catalyses cross-linking of glutamine and lysine residues in neuronal proteins. Loss of normal enzyme function is thought to disturb cytoskeletal cross-linking and protein homeostasis in Purkinje cells and other cerebellar neurons, leading to progressive Purkinje cell dysfunction and loss. The resulting cerebellar degeneration produces the ataxia, dysarthria and eye-movement abnormalities, while variable involvement of corticospinal and extrapyramidal pathways accounts for the pyramidal signs and dystonic or tremor features seen in some families.
additionalDifferentials: Repeat-expansion spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA1, 2, 3, 6, 7 and related types)
Spinocerebellar ataxia type 36 and other tremor-predominant dominant ataxias
Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) in older men
Autoimmune or gluten-related cerebellar ataxia (including anti-transglutaminase associations)
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to document cerebellar (and any brainstem) atrophy and exclude structural or acquired causes
Targeted molecular testing for common repeat-expansion SCAs before proceeding to TGM6 analysis
Next-generation sequencing ataxia gene panel or exome including TGM6
Detailed three-generation family history to establish autosomal dominant transmission
Screening for acquired ataxia causes (thyroid function, vitamin B12 and E, coeliac serology, alcohol history)
Nerve conduction studies where a sensory neuropathy or alternative diagnosis is suspected
redFlags: Rapid progression or early severe bulbar dysfunction, which should prompt reconsideration of an acquired or paraneoplastic cause
Prominent autonomic failure suggesting multiple system atrophy rather than a hereditary ataxia
Cognitive decline or seizures pointing to a broader neurodegenerative or metabolic process
Dysphagia with recurrent aspiration requiring swallow assessment and airway protection
reference.prognosis: SCA35 is slowly progressive over years to decades; many patients retain independent walking for a prolonged period, but cumulative cerebellar and pyramidal involvement can eventually lead to significant disability, dysarthria and dysphagia. Life expectancy is often relatively preserved, with prognosis influenced by bulbar involvement and fall-related complications.
pitfalls: Assuming a repeat-expansion SCA and stopping testing when common panels are negative, thereby missing a TGM6 variant
Overlooking the tremor or focal dystonic presentation and labelling the patient as essential tremor or a functional disorder
Attributing raised anti-transglutaminase antibodies solely to coeliac disease without considering the gene-antibody overlap in this ataxia
Interpreting isolated cerebellar atrophy on MRI as diagnostic when it is only supportive
Failing to offer genetic counselling regarding dominant inheritance and variable expressivity
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: With no disease-modifying therapy for this TGM6-related ataxia, base care on physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy
Treat the prominent postural and kinetic tremor with a trial of an anti-tremor agent such as a beta-blocker
Use botulinum toxin injections for focal dystonic features such as cervical dystonia, spasmodic dysphonia or writer's cramp
Apply antispasticity measures (physiotherapy and agents such as baclofen) for pyramidal involvement
Institute falls prevention and mobility aids, with swallow surveillance for dysarthria and dysphagia
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing for the autosomal dominant transmission
